title: The Farmer and the Fox
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Farmer was greatly annoyed by a Fox, which came prowling about his yard at night and carried off his fowls. So he set a trap for him and caught him; and in order to be revenged upon him, he tied a bunch of tow to his tail and set fire to it and let him go. As ill-luck would have it, however, the Fox made straight for the fields where the corn was standing ripe and ready for cutting. It quickly caught fire and was all burnt up, and the Farmer lost all his harvest. Revenge is a two-edged sword.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the Fox carrying off from the Farmer's yard?
options: His tools
His fowls
His firewood
His seed corn

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Farmer catch the Fox?
options: He chased him down on foot
He set a trap for him
He hired hunters with dogs
He waited by the henhouse with a gun

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Farmer tie to the Fox's tail?
options: A bunch of tow, which he set on fire
A heavy stone
A bell to warn the fowls
A rope tied to a stake

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where did the burning Fox run?
options: Into the farmhouse
Back to his den
Into the river
Into the fields where the corn was standing ripe

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Farmer lose in the end?
options: His fowls
His trap
All his harvest
His yard

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "prowling" mean in "came prowling about his yard at night"?
options: Sleeping quietly
Moving about stealthily in search of prey
Singing loudly
Digging a burrow

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the fire spread to the Farmer's own crop?
options: The Farmer accidentally dropped his torch in the field
The burning Fox happened to run through the ripe corn while trying to escape
The Fox deliberately set the field alight in revenge
Lightning struck the field at the same time

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, as its closing line suggests?
options: Foxes should never be trusted near a farm
An act of revenge can end up harming the one who takes it
Traps are the most reliable way to punish a thief
Fire is too dangerous a punishment for any crime

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the Farmer's feeling toward the Fox at the start?
options: He was greatly annoyed by him
He admired his cleverness
He felt sorry for him
He was afraid of him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Farmer do after tying tow to the Fox's tail and setting it alight?
options: He locked the Fox in a cage
He let him go
He drowned the fire immediately
He sold the Fox to a neighbor

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what condition was the corn in when the Fox ran into the fields?
options: Freshly planted
Standing ripe and ready for cutting
Already harvested and stored
Flooded from recent rain

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "ill-luck" mean in "As ill-luck would have it"?
options: Bad fortune
A clever plan
Great skill
A fair trade

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is ironic about how the Farmer's plan for revenge turned out?
options: The Fox forgave the Farmer afterward
The punishment meant for the Fox ended up destroying the Farmer's own harvest
The trap failed to catch the Fox at all
The Fox was completely unharmed by the fire

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Farmer traps a thieving Fox and sets him ablaze, but the fleeing Fox burns down the Farmer's own crop
A Farmer forgives a Fox for stealing his fowls
A Fox burns down a neighboring farm out of spite
A Farmer and a Fox become allies after a trap fails
